title: V. So Be It! So Be It!
paragraphs: The elder had been out of his cell for about twenty-five minutes. It was already past twelve-thirty, and Dmitri, the reason they had all gathered there, still had not appeared. He seemed almost forgotten, though, and when the elder came back in, he found his guests deep in lively conversation. Ivan and the two monks were doing most of the talking. Miüsov was trying to take part too, and quite eagerly, it seemed. But he had no luck at that either. He was plainly pushed into the background, and his remarks were ignored, which only made him more irritable. He had crossed swords with Ivan before, and he could not stand a certain offhandedness Ivan showed toward him.
“Up to now, at least, I have stood in the front ranks of everything progressive in Europe, and here the new generation simply ignores us,” he thought.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had given his word to sit still and keep quiet, had in fact kept quiet for some time. But he was watching his neighbor Miüsov with a mocking little smile, clearly enjoying his discomfort. He had been waiting a good while to settle old scores, and he was not going to let the chance slip. Leaning over Miüsov’s shoulder, he started teasing him again in a whisper.

“Why didn’t you leave just now, after the ‘courteously kissing’? Why did you agree to stay in such improper company? Because you felt insulted and wronged, and you stayed to prove yourself by showing off your brains. Now you won’t go until you’ve shown them what a mind you have.”
“You again?... On the contrary, I’m just leaving.”
“You’ll be the last, the last of all to go!” Fyodor Pavlovitch jabbed at him once more, almost at the very moment Father Zossima came back.

The discussion died down for a moment. The elder sat down in his old place and looked around at them all as if warmly inviting them to go on. Alyosha, who knew every expression of his face, saw that he was dreadfully tired and was forcing himself. Lately he had been prone to fainting fits from exhaustion. His face had the pallor that usually came before such attacks, and his lips were white. Yet he plainly did not want to break up the gathering. He seemed to have some purpose of his own in keeping them there. What purpose? Alyosha watched him closely.

“We were discussing this gentleman’s most interesting article,” said Father Iosif, the librarian, addressing the elder and nodding toward Ivan. “He puts forward a lot that is new, but I think the argument cuts both ways. It is an article written in reply to a book by a churchman on the question of the ecclesiastical court and how far its jurisdiction extends.”
“I’m sorry to say I haven’t read your article, though I’ve heard about it,” said the elder, giving Ivan a keen, steady look.
“He takes a most interesting position,” the Father Librarian went on. “As far as Church jurisdiction goes, he is apparently entirely opposed to the separation of Church and State.”
“That’s interesting. But in what sense?” Father Zossima asked Ivan.
At last Ivan answered him—not condescendingly, as Alyosha had feared, but modestly and with reserve, with obvious goodwill and, it seemed, without the slightest _arrière-pensée_.

“I start from the premise that this confusion of elements—that is, of the essential principles of Church and State—will of course go on forever, although it is impossible for them to mix, and although this confusion can lead to no consistent or even normal results, because there is falsehood at the very foundation of it. A compromise between the Church and the State on questions like jurisdiction is, I think, impossible in any real sense. My clerical opponent maintains that the Church holds a precise, defined position within the State. I maintain, on the contrary, that the Church ought to include the whole State and not merely occupy a corner of it. And if that is for some reason impossible at present, then it ought to be set up as the direct and chief aim of the future development of Christian society!”
“Quite right,” Father Païssy, the silent, learned monk, agreed firmly and warmly.
“Pure Ultramontanism!” Miüsov cried impatiently, crossing his legs one way and then the other.

“Oh, well, we have no mountains,” cried Father Iosif, and turning to the elder he went on: “Look at how he answers these ‘fundamental and essential’ propositions of his opponent, who is, mind you, a churchman. First: ‘No social organization can or ought to take it upon itself to dispose of the civic and political rights of its members.’ Second: ‘Criminal and civil jurisdiction ought not to belong to the Church, and does not fit its nature, either as a divine institution or as an organization of men for religious ends.’ And third and last: ‘The Church is a kingdom not of this world.’”

“What an unworthy play on words, and from a churchman!” Father Païssy could not stop himself from breaking in again. “I have read the book you answered,” he said to Ivan, “and I was astounded by the words ‘the Church is a kingdom not of this world.’ If it is not of this world, it cannot exist on earth at all. In the Gospel, the words ‘not of this world’ do not mean that. It is indefensible to play with words like this. Our Lord Jesus Christ came to establish the Church on earth. The Kingdom of Heaven, of course, is not of this world but in Heaven. Yet it can be entered only through the Church, which He founded and set up on earth. So a frivolous play on words here is unpardonable and improper. The Church is truly a kingdom, ordained to rule, and in the end it must surely become the kingdom that rules over all the earth. We have God’s promise of that.”
He stopped speaking suddenly, as if checking himself. After listening attentively and respectfully, Ivan went on, addressing the elder with perfect composure and the same ready cordiality as before:

“The whole point of my article is that during the first three centuries Christianity existed on earth only in the Church and was nothing but the Church. When the pagan Roman Empire wanted to become Christian, it inevitably happened that, in becoming Christian, it took in the Church but remained a pagan State in very many of its departments. In reality this was bound to happen. But Rome as a State kept too much of pagan civilization and culture—for example, in the very aims and fundamental principles of the State. The Christian Church, entering into the State, could of course give up no part of its fundamental principles—the rock on which it stands—and could pursue no aims other than those ordained and revealed by God Himself. Among them was that of drawing the whole world, and therefore the ancient pagan State itself, into the Church. In that way (that is, looking to the future), it is not the Church that should seek a definite position in the State, like ‘every social organization,’ or as ‘an organization of men for religious purposes’ (as my opponent calls the Church). On the contrary, every earthly State should in the end be completely transformed into the Church and become nothing but a Church, rejecting every purpose out of keeping with the aims of the Church. None of this will degrade it in any way, or take from its honor and glory as a great State, or from the glory of its rulers. It only turns it from a false, still pagan and mistaken path onto the true and rightful path, which alone leads to the eternal goal. That is why the author of the book _On the Foundations of Church Jurisdiction_ would have judged correctly if, in seeking and laying down those foundations, he had regarded them as a temporary compromise, unavoidable in our sinful and imperfect days. But as soon as the author ventures to declare that the foundations he now proposes, some of which Father Iosif just listed, are permanent, essential and eternal, he goes directly against the Church and its sacred and eternal vocation. That is the gist of my article.”

“In short,” Father Païssy began again, stressing each word, “certain theories, all too clearly formulated in the nineteenth century, say that the Church ought to turn into the State, as though that were progress from a lower form to a higher one. She would vanish into it and make room for science, for the spirit of the age, and for civilization. And if the Church resists and refuses, a corner will be set aside for her in the State, and even that under supervision. This is how it will be everywhere in modern Europe. But Russian hopes and ideas demand something else. They do not want the Church to pass into the State as from a lower type to a higher. They want the State to end by becoming worthy of being only the Church and nothing else. So be it! So be it!”

“Well, I must say you’ve reassured me somewhat,” Miüsov said with a smile, crossing his legs again. “So as I understand it, the realization of such an ideal is infinitely remote, at the second coming of Christ. That’s up to you. It’s a beautiful Utopian dream of the abolition of war, diplomacy, banks, and so on—something like socialism, in fact. But I imagined it was all meant seriously, and that the Church might be going to try criminals _now_, and sentence them to beatings, prison, and even death.”

“But if there were nothing but the ecclesiastical court, the Church would not sentence a criminal to prison or to death even now. Crime and the way it is viewed would inevitably change—not all at once, of course, but fairly soon,” Ivan replied calmly, without flinching.
“Are you serious?” Miüsov gave him a sharp look.

“If everything became the Church, the Church would exclude all the criminal and disobedient, and would not cut off their heads,” Ivan went on. “I ask you, what would become of the excluded man? He would then be cut off not only from men, as now, but from Christ. By his crime he would have sinned not only against men but against the Church of Christ. Strictly speaking, this is so even now, but it is not clearly stated, and very, very often the criminal of today comes to terms with his conscience: ‘I steal,’ he says, ‘but I don’t go against the Church. I’m not an enemy of Christ.’ That is what the criminal of today keeps telling himself. But when the Church takes the place of the State, it will be hard for him, standing against the Church all over the world, to say: ‘All men are mistaken, all in error, all mankind is the false Church. I, a thief and murderer, am the only true Christian Church.’ It will be very hard to say this to himself. It takes a rare combination of unusual circumstances. Now consider the other side, the Church’s own view of crime. Is it not bound to give up its present, almost pagan attitude? Is it not bound to change from the mechanical cutting off of its tainted member to protect society, as now, into wholly and honestly adopting the idea of the regeneration of the man, of his reformation and salvation?”

“What are you saying? I’m lost again,” Miüsov broke in. “Another sort of dream. Something shapeless, even impossible to grasp. What is this excommunication? What kind of exclusion? I suspect you’re just amusing yourself, Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, but you know, in reality it is so even now,” said the elder suddenly, and all turned to him at once. “Without the Church of Christ, nothing would hold the criminal back from doing evil, and there would be no real punishment for it afterward. I mean no punishment but the mechanical kind spoken of just now, which in most cases only embitters the heart. I mean not the real punishment, the only effective one, the only one that deters and softens, which lies in the conscience’s own recognition of sin.”
“How is that, may I ask?” Miüsov asked, with lively curiosity.

“Why,” began the elder, “all these sentences of exile with hard labor, and in the past with flogging too, reform no one. What is more, they hardly deter a single criminal, and crimes do not grow fewer but keep on increasing. You must admit that. So society is not made safe. The harmful member is cut off mechanically and sent far away, out of sight. But another criminal at once comes to take his place, and often two. If anything protects society, even in our time, and does regenerate and transform the criminal, it is only the law of Christ speaking in his conscience. Only when he sees his wrongdoing as a son of a Christian society—that is, of the Church—does he see his sin against society—that is, against the Church. So the criminal of today can recognize that he has sinned only against the Church, not against the State. If society, as a Church, held jurisdiction, it would know when to call a man back from exclusion and join him to itself again. But the Church has no real jurisdiction, only the power of moral condemnation, and so she of her own accord refrains from punishing the criminal in practice. She does not excommunicate him. She simply goes on exhorting him as a mother would. More than that, the Church tries to keep up full Christian fellowship with him. She lets him attend church services and receive the holy sacrament, she gives him alms, and she treats him more as a captive than as a convict. And what would become of the criminal, O Lord, if even Christian society—that is, the Church—rejected him, as the civil law rejects him and cuts him off? What would become of him if the Church punished him with excommunication as the direct consequence of the secular law? There could be no more terrible despair, at least for a Russian criminal, for Russian criminals still have faith. Yet who knows? Perhaps something fearful would happen then. Perhaps the criminal’s despairing heart would lose its faith, and then what would become of him? But the Church, like a tender, loving mother, keeps back from active punishment herself, because the sinner is already punished too severely by the civil law, and someone at least must have pity on him. Above all, the Church keeps back because her judgment alone holds the truth. So it cannot be joined, in practice or in morals, to any other judgment, even as a temporary compromise. She can make no bargain over that. The foreign criminal, they say, rarely repents, since the very doctrines of today persuade him that his crime is no crime, only a reaction against an unjustly oppressive force. Society cuts him off completely, by a force that overpowers him mechanically. (So at least they say of themselves in Europe.) It accompanies this exclusion with hatred, forgetfulness, and the deepest indifference to the final fate of the erring brother. So it all happens without the compassionate intervention of the Church, for in many places there are no churches at all. Churchmen and splendid church buildings remain, but the churches themselves long ago strove to pass from Church into State and disappear into it entirely. So it seems, at least, in Lutheran countries. As for Rome, it was proclaimed a State instead of a Church a thousand years ago. And so the criminal no longer feels himself a member of the Church, and sinks into despair. If he returns to society, he often does so with such hatred that society itself instinctively cuts him off. You can judge for yourself how it must end. In many cases it might seem to be the same with us. But the difference is that, besides the established law courts, we have the Church too, which always keeps up its bond with the criminal as a dear and still precious son. And there is something more. The judgment of the Church is still preserved, though only in thought. It no longer exists in practice, but it lives on as a dream for the future, and the criminal, no doubt, recognizes it instinctively in his soul. What was said here just now is also true: if the jurisdiction of the Church were brought into practice in its full force—if the whole of society were changed into the Church—then the Church’s judgment would influence the reformation of the criminal as it never does now. Possibly, too, crimes themselves would become incredibly fewer. And there can be no doubt that the Church would regard the criminal, and the crime of the future, quite differently in many cases. She would succeed in restoring the excluded, in restraining those who plan evil, and in raising up the fallen. It is true,” said Father Zossima, with a smile, “Christian society is not ready now and rests only on some seven righteous men. But since they are never lacking, it will stand unshaken, awaiting its complete transformation from a society almost heathen in character into a single, universal and all-powerful Church. So be it, so be it! Even if it comes at the end of the ages, for it is ordained to come to pass! And there is no need to be troubled about times and seasons, for the secret of the times and seasons lies in the wisdom of God, in His foresight and His love. What seems still far off by human reckoning may, by Divine ordinance, be close at hand, on the eve of its appearing. And so be it, so be it!”
“So be it, so be it!” Father Païssy repeated sternly and reverently.
“Strange, extremely strange!” Miüsov declared, not so much with heat as with suppressed indignation.
“What strikes you as so strange?” Father Iosif asked cautiously.

“Why, it’s out of all bounds!” cried Miüsov, suddenly bursting out. “The State is abolished and the Church is raised to the rank of the State. It’s not just Ultramontanism, it’s arch-Ultramontanism! Pope Gregory the Seventh never dreamed of such a thing!”

“You have got it completely wrong,” said Father Païssy sternly. “Understand this: the Church is not to be turned into the State. That is Rome and its dream. That is the devil’s third temptation. It is the other way around. The State is turned into the Church. It will rise and become a Church over the whole world. That is the exact opposite of Ultramontanism and Rome, and of your reading of it. It is simply the glorious destiny ordained for the Orthodox Church. This star will rise in the east!”

Miüsov said nothing, and the silence was pointed. Everything about him spoke of extraordinary personal dignity. A superior, patronizing smile played on his lips. Alyosha watched it all, his heart pounding. The whole conversation had shaken him deeply. In passing, he glanced at Rakitin, who stood rooted to his spot by the door, listening and watching closely, though his eyes were lowered. Alyosha guessed from the color in his cheeks that Rakitin was probably just as excited, and he knew what excited him.

“Allow me to tell you a little anecdote, gentlemen,” Miüsov said impressively, with a peculiarly majestic air. “Some years ago, soon after the _coup d’état_ of December, I happened to be calling in Paris on an extremely influential figure in the Government, and at his house I met a very interesting man. He was not exactly a detective, but a sort of superintendent over a whole regiment of political detectives—a rather powerful position in its own way. Curiosity prompted me to seize the chance to talk with him. He had not come as a visitor but as a subordinate bringing a special report, and he saw the reception his chief gave me. So he condescended to speak with some openness—to a certain extent only, of course. He was more courteous than open, as Frenchmen know how to be courteous, especially to a foreigner. But I understood him perfectly. The subject was the socialist revolutionaries, who were being persecuted at that time. I will quote only one most curious remark this man let drop. ‘We are not particularly afraid,’ he said, ‘of all these socialists, anarchists, infidels and revolutionists. We keep watch on them and know all their doings. But there are a few peculiar men among them who believe in God and are Christians, yet are socialists all the same. Those are the people we fear most. They are dreadful people! The socialist who is a Christian is more to be dreaded than a socialist who is an atheist.’ The words struck me at the time, and now they have suddenly come back to me here, gentlemen.”
“You apply them to us, and take us for socialists?” Father Païssy asked bluntly, without beating about the bush.

But before Pyotr Alexandrovitch could think what to answer, the door opened and the long-awaited guest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, came in. They had in fact given up expecting him, and his sudden appearance caused a moment of surprise.
